[MUQATIL:19:41-44/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The knowledge that came to Ibrahim is clarification of what happens after death; he asks his father to follow his religion on a just, straight path, meaning Islam.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالجزاءإذاأدخلتفيهألفالاستفهام)#486/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The interrogative hamza can precede a conditional construction such as أإن تأتني آتك; من and متى already function as conditional particles and need the hamza added to form a question.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالجزاءإذاأدخلتفيهألفالاستفهام)#486/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The hamza does not change the clause's syntax and can enter clauses with different case forms; هل instead starts a new clause and cannot be inserted the same way.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالجزاءإذاأدخلتفيهألفالاستفهام)#486/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yūnus regards أإن تأتني آتيك as awkward in a conditional construction, though acceptable as an interrogative.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالجزاءإذاأدخلتفيهألفالاستفهام)#486/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sībawayh treats أفإن مت as a genuine conditional after the hamza; if إن were not conditional, its placement would be awkward, while reversing the order would also work. | mentions 21:34
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحروفالتيلاتقدمفيهاالأسماءالفعل)#492/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Particles governing verbs normally must touch the verb; separation by a noun is forbidden and is especially poor with jussive particles, which are fewer than noun-governing particles.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحروفالتيلاتقدمفيهاالأسماءالفعل)#492/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Conditional particles generally resist a subject placed before the verb, by analogy with jussive operators, but their broader uses permit such separation in poetry.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحروفالتيلاتقدمفيهاالأسماءالفعل)#492/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With إن not pronounced jussive, a noun may separate it from its verb in ordinary speech; a jussive form is poetic because it resembles لم.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحروفالتيلاتقدمفيهاالأسماءالفعل)#492/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | إن, as the original conditional particle, permits separation and ellipsis, as in the shorthand إن خيرا فخير وإن شرا فشر.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحروفالتيلاتقدمفيهاالأسماءالفعل)#492/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · عدي بن زيد | reports | ʿAdī ibn Zayd's verse uses a jussive response after متى with a separated subject, an example of the poetic license Sibawayh describes.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحروفالتيلاتقدمفيهاالأسماءالفعل)#492/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · كعب بن جعبل | reports | Kaʿb ibn Jaʿbal's line likewise has a jussive after أينما with a separated subject; Sibawayh says a finite verb would be stronger.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحروفالتيلاتقدمفيهاالأسماءالفعل)#492/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A raised verb after إن is understood through an underlying verb; a noun after the conditional must begin an independent topic-comment clause, not serve as a direct nominal start.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحروفالتيلاتقدمفيهاالأسماءالفعل)#492/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A subject clause after the conditional may be parsed as an independent topic-comment construction, analogous to زيدا ضربته; a following فانا clause makes this reading clear.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالحروفالتيلاتقدمفيهاالأسماءالفعل)#492/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | If the independent-clause analysis is not adopted, raising after the conditional is limited to poetry, as in the examples including Hishām al-Marmī's line.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكونفيهالأسماءالتييجازيبهابمنزلةالذي)#483/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A conditional noun becomes relative-like when إن or كان already governs the construction; those operators cannot be left without a syntactic role, and doubling the conditional particle would be impossible.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكونفيهالأسماءالتييجازيبهابمنزلةالذي)#483/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The addressee ending cannot be silently supplied in كان or its sisters: ليس من يأتك تعطه cannot mean لست, nor can كان stand for كنت without its pronoun.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكونفيهالأسماءالتييجازيبهابمنزلةالذي)#483/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Al-Aʿshā's أن هالك كل من يحفى وينتعل is understood as أنه هالك, another example of an omitted هاء.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكونفيهالأسماءالتييجازيبهابمنزلةالذي)#483/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Lightened أن in قد علمت أن لا يقول ذاك means أنه لا يقول; Qur'an 20:89 uses the same ellipsis. The لا can compensate for the lost marker, though this pattern is less strong. | mentions 20:89
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكونفيهالأسماءالتييجازيبهابمنزلةالذي)#483/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When من, إن, or أي is not occupied by another governor, it can retain its conditional force.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكونفيهالأسماءالتييجازيبهابمنزلةالذي)#483/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An explicit subject pronoun in كان or ليس permits a conditional clause, as in كنت من يأتني آته; without it, من is relative-like.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكونفيهالأسماءالتييجازيبهابمنزلةالذي)#483/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Al-Khalīl explains al-Aʿshā's conditional poem by supplying an understood إنه; without that pronoun, the construction would be impossible.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكونفيهالأسماءالتييجازيبهابمنزلةالذي)#483/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Al-Aʿshā's إن من لام في بني بنت حسان is cited as a conditional construction whose omitted هاء is understood.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكونفيهالأسماءالتييجازيبهابمنزلةالذي)#483/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Al-Rāʿī's فلو أن ... وإن كان سرح ... supports the implicit-pronoun analysis; without intended هاء, the wording would be impossible.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكونفيهالأسماءالتييجازيبهابمنزلةالذي)#483/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After علمت, من يأتني آته also contains an implicit هاء; the light form أن is admitted here only on that analysis.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكونفيهالأسماءالتييجازيبهابمنزلةالذي)#483/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | ʿAdī ibn Zayd's أن كلانا illustrates the light form with an understood pronoun.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابيذهبفيهالجزاءمنالأسماء)#484/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After particles such as إذ that leave the clause unchanged, a conditional response is normally not jussive because that construction is not its proper syntactic place.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابيذهبفيهالجزاءمنالأسماء)#484/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | إن كان in the Qur'anic construction is acceptable because it is not jussive, like an ordinary clause followed by إن فعلت. | mentions 56:90, 56:91
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابيذهبفيهالجزاءمنالأسماء)#484/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Poetry may use a jussive response after these unchanged particles; Labīd supplies an example after إذ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابيذهبفيهالجزاءمنالأسماء)#484/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A pronoun can intervene between إذ and من, paralleling a noun between كان and من, while the conditional clause remains intact.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابيذهبفيهالجزاءمنالأسماء)#484/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After فإذا, jussive agreement is possible when a pronoun is understood; without that implied pronoun, إذا itself fills the conditional role and jussive is excluded.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابيذهبفيهالجزاءمنالأسماء)#484/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In لا من يأتك تعطه, لا is semantically light like ما and leaves the following construction unchanged, so it does not license a jussive response.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابيذهبفيهالجزاءمنالأسماء)#484/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The particle لا is لغو like ما in فبما رحمة من الله لنت لهم: it does not alter the case or syntactic state of what follows. | mentions 3:159
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابيذهبفيهالجزاءمنالأسماء)#484/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The occurrence of إن after لا supports a jussive construction after لا, distinguishing this use from لا as a merely light particle.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابيذهبفيهالجزاءمنالأسماء)#484/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A conditional after ولكن is acceptable when an implicit subject is recoverable, just as after إذا; Ṭarafa's line illustrates the construction with متى.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابيذهبفيهالجزاءمنالأسماء)#484/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In al-ʿUjayr al-Salūlī's line, ما is لغو and أملك is governed by متى as the conditional clause; متى does not connect to a following clause as من does.
[SIBAWAYH:فإذابنيتالاسمعليهقلتضربتزيداوهوالحدلأنكتريدأنتعملهوتحمل#48/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The normal order ضربت زيدا lets the verb govern its object directly; Sībawayh calls it the standard construction.
[SIBAWAYH:فإذابنيتالاسمعليهقلتضربتزيداوهوالحدلأنكتريدأنتعملهوتحمل#48/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | زيد مررت به is farther from direct accusative fronting because the pronoun is separated from the verb by a preposition; it resembles زيد لقيت أخاه.
[SIBAWAYH:فإذابنيتالاسمعليهقلتضربتزيداوهوالحدلأنكتريدأنتعملهوتحمل#48/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A related object can license accusative fronting because acting on a person's relative is like acting on that person; Sībawayh cites humiliating or honoring someone's brother.
[SIBAWAYH:فإذابنيتالاسمعليهقلتضربتزيداوهوالحدلأنكتريدأنتعملهوتحمل#48/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | prefers | In زيدا لقيت أخاه the accusative is an illustrative, unspoken-like paraphrase of a relation to Zayd; nominative is clearer and better.
[SIBAWAYH:فإذابنيتالاسمعليهقلتضربتزيداوهوالحدلأنكتريدأنتعملهوتحمل#48/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The same alternatives occur with أيهم: أيهم تر يأتك is accusative by an understood repetition, parallel to the fronted Zayd construction.
[SIBAWAYH:فإذابنيتالاسمعليهقلتضربتزيداوهوالحدلأنكتريدأنتعملهوتحمل#48/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Fronting the object as زيدا ضربت is equally good; emphasis and concern determine order rather than grammaticality.
[SIBAWAYH:فإذابنيتالاسمعليهقلتضربتزيداوهوالحدلأنكتريدأنتعملهوتحمل#48/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When a verb is built on a topic, as in زيد ضربته, the resumptive pronou

n is required; the topic is like a مبتدأ receiving its predicate.
[SIBAWAYH:فإذابنيتالاسمعليهقلتضربتزيداوهوالحدلأنكتريدأنتعملهوتحمل#48/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A fronted accusative such as زيدا ضربته can instead depend on an omitted verb understood from the following verb; the first verb is suppressed because the second explains it.
[SIBAWAYH:فإذابنيتالاسمعليهقلتضربتزيداوهوالحدلأنكتريدأنتعملهوتحمل#48/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Bishr ibn Abī Khāzim's line about تميم is transmitted with both accusative and nominative readings.
[SIBAWAYH:فإذابنيتالاسمعليهقلتضربتزيداوهوالحدلأنكتريدأنتعملهوتحمل#48/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | prefers | The accusative is common in the poem, but the nominative is better when the poet intends direct verbal government, which favors a nearer object.
[SIBAWAYH:فإذابنيتالاسمعليهقلتضربتزيداوهوالحدلأنكتريدأنتعملهوتحمل#48/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Dhū al-Rumma's line about Ibn Abī Mūsā gives another poetic example of the fronted noun construction.
[SIBAWAYH:فإذابنيتالاسمعليهقلتضربتزيداوهوالحدلأنكتريدأنتعملهوتحمل#48/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أعطيت allows the same patterns as ضربت: a fronted object, a following object, or a topic resumed by a pronoun.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p226/r5] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | The knowledge that came to Abraham means prophethood, and the straight path he offers is an upright religion, Islam, leading to Paradise.
[TAB-FULL:v15p550/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Abraham says God gave him knowledge his father lacked and asks him to follow; he will guide him to an upright path, God's unbent religion, on which one does not stray.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p332/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Ibrahim's saying that knowledge came to him indicates that revelation had come to him.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p332/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | صراطا سويا means a straight path.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p152/r8] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · author | holds | Mujahid lists added yāʾs left unvowelled before a separate alif when attached to a jussive verb, including فاذكروني أذكركم and رب فأنظرني.
[SULAMI:v1p427#2/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · القاسم | reports | The way to God is following: the highest follow scripture, then the Messenger, then the Companions, then God's friends and those learned in God; following is the safest path.
[SULAMI:v1p427#2/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · سهل بن عبد الله | reports | Imitation is hardest on the ego because it offers the ego no breath or ease.
[THALABI:v6p216#2/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Abraham’s God-given knowledge and clear proof concern the afterlife and punishment of those who worship other than God; following Abraham leads to an upright path.
[QUSHAYRI:v2p242/r3] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Abraham urges his father to follow because truth is more strongly with him despite his younger age; salvation is following truth's people, ruin lies in innovation and false paths.
[QUSHAYRI:v2p242/r6] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Abraham showed every form of compassion, but repeated counsel did not help his father because later effort cannot undo a prior decree of exclusion.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p254/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | The knowledge Abraham received means certainty and recognition of God.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p254/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abraham's statement that knowledge came to him indicates that he had received revelation.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p254/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Following Abraham means following what came to him from his Lord so that the father will be guided to a straight religion.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p216/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | When a negated sentence contains a restriction or qualification, the negation applies specifically to that restriction rather than automatically denying the whole event.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p216/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Negating that all people came means some came; it cannot mean nobody came, just as negating that they came together implies they came separately.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p216/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The same focus applies affirmatively: in saying everyone came, كل supplies the informative point, since the uncertainty concerns whether the whole group came.
[JISHUMI:v6p4564/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · غير مسمى | reports | The knowledge Abraham received may be religious knowledge, knowledge of resurrection, or knowledge of God's promise, threat, and punishment for worshipping another.
[JISHUMI:v6p4564/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · غير مسمى | reports | Knowledge may mean its means: evidence, revelation, and prophethood.
[JISHUMI:v6p4564/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Ṣirāṭan sawiyyan is an upright path of truth; other views call it the road to Paradise or escape from Hell.
[JISHUMI:v6p4566/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The passage refutes the view of the أصحاب المعارف because Abraham says he received knowledge his father lacked.
[JISHUMI:v6p4566/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Those given knowledge must invite others and clarify religion.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p234/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The knowledge that came to Abraham is knowledge of God and spiritual recognition; following him leads to a straight path.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p21/r12] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Each of Abraham's four counsels begins yā-abati as a plea for closeness and compassion.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p21/r13] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | In mā lā yasmaʿ and mā lam ya'tika, mā may be relative or descriptive; the object of 'hears' and 'sees' is omitted and not intended.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p21/r16] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The wording that knowledge 'came' to Abraham implies that his knowledge was newly acquired.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p21/r7] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Abraham next invites his father gently to truth without calling him ignorant or himself exceptionally learned; he says he has some guidance his father lacks and can lead him safely.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p18/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Abraham's phrase “knowledge has come to me” indicates this conversation occurred after he became a prophet.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p18/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The balanced straight path is the path of faith.
[TABRISI:19:41-44/r15] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Ibrahim says he received knowledge and recognition of God his father had not received, and promises a straight, moderate path.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p352/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | Sawī is derived from evenness and uprightness, used of physical form, religion, and a path; the shared idea is uprightness.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p352/r4] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل التفسير | reports | A third sense is just or right: Abraham promises to guide his father to an upright path, also called the right path in Ṭā Hā. | mentions 20:135
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p236#3/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The knowledge Abraham received includes knowledge of and recognition of God, which his father had not received.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p55#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi divides two coordinated verbs followed by an eligible noun into four cases, based on whether their functions are alike or different and whether the noun is singular or plural.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p55#2/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · البصريون | prefers | Basrans add ما جاءني من أحد: the governing particle is nearer to the noun than the verb, so proximity favors it.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p55#2/r11] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · البصريون | prefers | Their general argument is that neither ignoring both verbs nor applying both is possible, so proximity favors the nearer one.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p55#2/r12] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الكوفيون | prefers | Kufans extend their dual-and-plural argument to singular nouns: since second-verb governance entails anticipatory pronominal reference in those cases, the first should govern here too.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p55#2/r13] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الكوفيون | prefers | Kufans say the first verb encounters the noun without obstruction, whereas the second finds it already governed, so the unobstructed first should prevail.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p55#2/r14] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | For a dual or plural noun, if the second verb governs, the first takes a matching subject suffix; if the first governs, the second takes it and the noun is accusative.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p55#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ allows two verbs to govern one singular noun, as in قام وقعد زيد; the common view forbids this because one effect cannot have two causes.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p55#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The defense that two explanatory causes yield one recognition does not resolve the objection, since recognition itself results from the combined causes.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p55#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · البصريون | prefers | With two verbs and a dual or plural noun, Basrans prefer the nearer second verb to govern; the first then carries an implicit pronoun.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p55#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الكوفيون | prefers | Kufans prefer the first verb because letting the second govern forces a pronoun in the first before its referent is mentioned.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p55#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · البصريون | prefers | When two verbs demand different effects and a singular noun follows, Basrans again choose the nearer governor, while Kufans disagree.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p55#2/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الكوفيون | rejects | Kufans answer that these examples prove only that the nearer verb can govern, not that the farther verb is impossible.
[RAZI-FULL:v21p192#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | An objection says that only a complete, infallible prophet or imam can guide someone to grasp the proofs, so Abraham’s invitation seems to concede the need for such a guide.
[RAZI-FULL:v21p192#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | The response denies that a prophet is necessary

[BAYDAWI-FULL:19:43-45/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Idol worship is effectively worship of Satan because he commands it; Satan disobeys the Lord who bestowed every blessing, and an obedient follower shares the rebel’s fault.
